articles.title_orig: China's Treasury Pile Is Shrinking on Paper. The Custody Data Tell a Different Story
articles.title_zh: China's Treasury Pile Is Shrinking on Paper. The Custody Data Tell a Different Story
articles.content_orig:
americannewsgroup.com /sp/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"> americannewsgroup.com /sp/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">American News Group News Commentary - China held $590.7 billion of U.S. Treasury securities at the end of August, down from $699.7 billion a year earlier, according to U.S. Treasury data released Friday. Fortune called it the lowest level in 18 years, and for anyone watching de-dollarization , the trend looks clear. But over the same year, holdings attributed to Belgium and Canada kept climbing, and a former Treasury official who follows the data says some of China's bonds may simply be sitting in someone else's vault. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: The Bank of New York Mellon Corporation (NYSE: BNY), State Street Corporation (NYSE: STT), iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ: TLT), CME Group Inc. (NASDAQ: CME), SPDR Gold Shares (NYSE Arca: GLD ).
The catch is in how the numbers are collected. The Treasury Department gathers the data mainly from U.S.-based custodians and broker-dealers, and U.S. securities held in overseas custody accounts may not be attributed to their actual owners. That leaves room for a country's holdings to show up under the name of whichever financial center is holding them.
Belgium was credited with $490.5 billion of Treasuries in August, up from $451.1 billion a year earlier. Canada held $464.6 billion, up from $444.0 billion, and Fortune noted Canada's total stood at $169 billion five years ago. Brad Setser of the Council on Foreign Relations, a former Treasury official, told Fortune that "it seems likely that China is now using multiple non-U.S. custodians to mask its true holdings." In a post on X, he added that "the evidence that China uses a Canadian custodian for some of its Agencies is especially strong," referring to bonds issued by U.S. federal housing agencies.
That puts a spotlight on the global custody business, where large banks safekeep and service trillions of dollars of securities for central banks, pension funds and asset managers. BNY reported $63.4 trillion in assets under custody and/or administration at Sept. 30, up 10% from a year earlier, as third-quarter revenue rose 12% to $5.7 billion and diluted earnings per share climbed 24% to $2.34. "BNY delivered strong results in the third quarter," CEO Robin Vince said in the Oct. 15 release. The shares rose 0.41% last week, from $142.71 at the Oct. 9 close to $143.30 on Oct. 16, according to Stock Analysis data.
State Street reported $59.2 trillion in assets under custody and/or administration at the end of the third quarter, up 14.5% from a year earlier, with assets under management up 15.8% to $6.3 trillion. Revenue rose 12.9% to $4.0 billion and diluted earnings per share rose 32.7% to $3.69. Even so, the shares fell 4.14% on Oct. 14, the day the results came out, and finished the week down 5.28% at $165.72.
Fortune also reported that China has reduced its long-term Treasuries while increasing short-term bills. Across all foreign holders, the picture in August was mixed. Total foreign holdings of Treasuries rose to $9.33 trillion from $9.25 trillion a year earlier, and foreign investors made $300.7 billion of net purchases of long-term U.S. securities in the month, even as they cut their holdings of Treasury bills by $47.8 billion. Japan remained the largest holder at $1.07 trillion, followed by the United Kingdom at $1.01 trillion.
Long bonds rallied last week. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, which holds about $47 billion in assets, rose 2.65% from $77.98 to $80.05.
The trading activity around government debt has been heavy. CME Group reported record third-quarter average daily volume of 29.4 million contracts, up 16% from a year earlier, including record interest rate volume. U.S. Treasury futures and options averaged 9.4 million contracts a day in the quarter, up 25%, and 9.5 million in September, up 42%. CME shares gained 4.74% last week to $293.87.
CONTINUED... Read more market coverage at: americannewsgroup.com
Part of the story is diversification. U.S. sanctions against Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine encouraged the People's Bank of China and other central banks to move away from dollar reserves and toward alternatives such as gold, Fortune reported. In September, the People's Bank of China added to its gold reserves for a 23rd consecutive month, its largest monthly purchase since September 2023.
For investors who want gold exposure without a vault, the SPDR Gold Shares fund holds about $141 billion in assets and charges a 0.40% expense ratio. It slipped 0.67% last week, from $384.58 to $382.01, after rising 1.79% on Oct. 15.
Meanwhile, China's trade surplus keeps growing. Its customs agency reported a trade surplus of $938.1 billion for the first nine months of 2026, including $133.5 billion in September alone, as exports jumped 36.3% from a year earlier, the Associated Press reported. That followed a 2025 surplus of $1.2 trillion, the largest in recorded history, according to Fortune. Setser estimates that U.S. financial assets still make up 50% to 55% of China's reserve portfolio.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.content_orig:
Iran's Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard met Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Doha on Monday to discuss energy relations and cooperation between the two countries.
According to Iran's official news agency IRNA , al-Kaabi confirmed the meeting, which focused on bilateral energy ties and opportunities for cooperation.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's government-controlled Shabwa province rose to 50 on Monday, a government official told the French news agency AFP, after military sources earlier put the toll at more than 30.
The Iran-backed rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," said Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa.
He added that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to facilities in neighbouring Hadramout and Aden.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen on Monday, killing at least 20 soldiers, two Yemeni military officials said.
The rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that left at least two dozen more troops wounded, the officials said.
The military officials with the internationally recognized government of Yemen spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.
Yemen's decade-long civil war has intensified and become intertwined with the wider regional conflict sparked by the U.S. war with Iran over the last few months, as the Houthis, considered one of Iran's most potent proxy forces, attacks the government's Saudi backers on their home turf.
Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure, including civilian airports, have killed more than 20 people in recent weeks, and President Trump has said he's considering joining Saudi operations against the rebels. The Houthis have warned that if the U.S. does intervene, it would prompt a  "swift and painful" retaliation against U.S. personnel and interests across the region.
Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel and benchmark U.S. crude dropping 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.
The prices fell after President Trump late Friday signed an executive order to put new U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing disappointment from Ukraine , with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.
Mr. Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a diesel deal with Russia in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
But despite Mr. Trump's controversial efforts to ease energy costs for Americans, oil prices have remained much higher compared to before the Iran war, due in large part to the ongoing risks to the supply chain caused by the crisis in the Middle East .
On Friday the price of Brent crude hit nearly $110 a barrel, its highest level since mid-May.
A tug boat traveling near the Strait of Hormuz was struck by two unknown projectiles, a British maritime monitoring agency said Sunday .
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said in a statement that a tugboat traveling southbound off the coast of the United Arab Emirates "reported being struck by two unknown projectiles."
"The tug has sustained damage but is continuing on its route," the agency said, "one minor casualty has been reported."
Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the strait, according to the UKMTO, which said October has already become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March.
The U.S. issued a security alert on Monday urging Americans in the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance."
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," the statement said.
It added that hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly and that groups backed by Iran may target U.S. interests overseas "or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world."
At least 20 people, including one American, were killed in one week in October when Houthi rebels attacked Saudi airports.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was expected to pay his first visit to Iran on Monday since the U.S. and Israel sparked the ongoing war with the Islamic Republic by launching joint strikes on Feb. 28.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Sunday that the two sides would discuss "regional and international developments," while Lavrov said his visit was "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war."
Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Iran presented a seven-day ceasefire proposal in late September that called for an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a return to direct negotiations on Tehran's nuclear program. President Trump rejected the proposal, which Iran says remains on the table.
Conflict raged between the Houthis and the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Iran-backed rebel group on Sunday, as both sides traded strikes.
In Riyadh, where intensifying violence has disrupted life for residents, the landmark Kingdom Centre skyscraper ordered "mandatory" remote working for office tenants until further notice. Although a reason for the order wasn't provided, it followed a security alert and two drone interceptions around the capital city, in addition to a number of attacks by Houthis on Saudi targets in recent weeks.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition, which backs the internationally-recognized government in war-wracked Yemen, has launched repeated air raids on regions of the country that Houthis control. One alleged Saudi airstrike in northern Yemen  killed at least nine people and wounded 16 others on Sunday, the Houthis' Saba news agency reported.
The coalition said Sunday that two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed in Najran, near the Yemen border, blaming a "technical malfunction" for the incident. The Houthis said they "downed an Apache helicopter belonging to the Saudi enemy" in the same area.
Iran's foreign minister said Sunday that Tehran's conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have not changed, but that its proposal for a limited ceasefire with the U.S. to reopen the vital waterway remains on the table.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency on Sunday that Tehran is still reviewing "comments" from the U.S. on the Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that was first presented in September, but rejected by President Trump .
"If they comply with our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will begin on the seventh day," Araghchi said, referring to the timeline proposed by Iran, which calls for the U.S. to lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and to ease sanctions on the country, among other concessions.
"Our conditions are fair, and if the United States is willing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, it can meet them within a few days," Araghchi said.

articles.title_orig: Oil Futures Pull Back on Russia Sanctions Waiver
articles.title_zh: Oil Futures Pull Back on Russia Sanctions Waiver
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices fell more than 2% on Monday, October 19, after President Donald Trump waived new sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia, raising expectations of additional Russian fuel exports. However, continuing tanker attacks in the Middle East kept Brent crude above $107 per barrel.
The pullback followed Trump's October 16 executive order suspending sanctions and tariffs under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a significant policy shift as Washington attempts to contain rising energy costs.
Under the White House executive order , Trump waived specified sanctions and import duties established by the Graham Act, including measures targeting countries purchasing Russian energy.
The decision does not remove every existing U.S. sanction on Russia. Nevertheless, it reduces the immediate threat of additional trade penalties that could restrict Russian energy sales.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated that the administration could take up to 60 days to assess the economic consequences before determining further action.
The waiver follows an earlier agreement allowing additional Russian diesel exports, which had already contributed to an oil price decline on October 13.
However, additional Russian fuel shipments would not necessarily translate into equivalent increases in global crude production.
Russia's refinery infrastructure has suffered repeated disruptions, and the International Energy Agency has warned that diesel shortages could persist into 2027 despite efforts to restore supplies.
The impact of Washington's policy change remains constrained by continuing disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz.
Reuters reported that an oil tanker caught fire and exploded after striking a naval mine in the southern strait on Sunday, according to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The latest incident renewed concerns about vessel safety along one of the world's most important energy shipping routes.
Oil flows through the strait remain far below pre-conflict levels, with Reuters reporting a decline from more than 20 million barrels per day to approximately 8.5 million barrels.
Although Gulf exports previously recovered as producers developed alternative shipping arrangements, continued attacks have complicated efforts to restore reliable transportation.
The risks have also increased freight and insurance expenses. Some tanker operators have reportedly offered crew bonuses reaching $25,000 for dangerous Gulf voyages.
Consequently, falling benchmark prices do not necessarily mean refiners immediately receive cheaper physical oil.
The market now faces two competing forces: the possibility of greater Russian energy availability and the continued threat of Middle Eastern supply disruptions.
Further progress toward restoring Hormuz shipping could weaken crude prices, particularly if additional Russian exports materialize. Another major tanker incident, however, could quickly reverse Monday's decline.
Physical market pressures remain especially important. Chevron CEO Mike Wirth recently warned that crude delivered to Asia could cost substantially more than benchmark futures because of shipping risks and regional shortages.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500, Nasdaq open higher as AI stocks rebound ahead of major earnings
articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq open higher as AI stocks rebound ahead of major earnings
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite rose on Monday as traders moved back into tech following last week's artificial intelligence-related rout.
The tech-heavy index added 1.4%, while the S&P 500 gained 0.7%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 52 points, or 0.1%.
Intel advanced 5% after JPMorgan analysts upgraded their rating on the chipmaker. Advanced Micro Devices and Micron Technology were also up 3% and 4%, respectively.
The S&P 500 lost nearly 2% last week — its biggest weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, snapping a four-week winning streak. Information technology also shed more than 6% to post its worst weekly performance since April 2025. It was the most net sold global sector last week , with hedge funds selling the largest percentage of tech on record, per Goldman Sachs.
Concerns around the health of the AI trade took center stage after CNBC reported, citing sources, that Anthropic's third-quarter revenue totaled $16.8 billion . And while that's up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, it raised flags among investors about the pace of growth with the AI build-out.
Investors in the corporate bond market have started to shun CoreWeave, with the company's credit default swaps reaching distress levels .
Goldman Sachs traders noted Friday: "AI Credit Spreads and hyperscalers specifically are at the widest levels of the year. The last time spreads were nearly this high, the underlying equities were 15% lower."
"The widening across the complex has forced investors to confront what happens as AI spending growth slows. AI Capex has likely peaked and financing, sustainability, and returns on capital have become the debate rather than the next near term earnings revision," they said. "Pessimism is increasing, market breadth is low, and [Friday] we saw the second highest amount of puts traded (right behind June of this year)."
Traders were also keeping a wary eye on oil markets with ship attacks in the Persian Gulf picking up and Ukraine and Russia trading attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine hit an oil terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia on Sunday. Longer-dated oil futures have begun to ratchet higher on expectations energy infrastructure disruptions may last well into 2027.
On Monday, however, Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures were both trading slightly lower. Brent fell more than 1% to trade almost $108 per barrel, while WTI was around 1% lower at around $100.
A slew of earnings from major companies such as Meta Platforms and Tesla hit the Street this week, with optimism those results will stabilize the market.
U.S. homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level since June 2012 in October, as rising mortgage rates, energy and material costs, and worsening labor and lot conditions continue to weigh on housing demand.
The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) and Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) dropped three points to 29 in October, its lowest reading since June 2012. The index remains well below the key 50-point threshold that signals positive sentiment.
"Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges," said NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz.
Dietz said that while demand persists, higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.
"As a result, buyer traffic has fallen to its lowest level since April 2012, excluding the pandemic's onset in April 2020," he said.
Neocloud CoreWeave rolled over into the red during morning trading on Monday after rising in premarket trading. Shares were just below flat as of 10:09 a.m.
CoreWeave sold off in a major way last week, dropping 25% on profitability concerns related to the ongoing artificial intelligence buildout. Other neoclouds, which are AI-dedicated providers of computing power, followed suit, including Nebius and IREN.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began the week in positive territory.
The broad market index rose 0.5% shortly after the opening bell, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq advanced 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 63 points, or 0.1%.
The S&P 500 information technology sector saw substantial pressure last week amid a sell-off of artificial intelligence-related names , according to Goldman Sachs.
In a recent note, the firm said that the sector — which saw a more than 6% drop in the week ended Oct. 16 — was "by far the most net sold global sector" last week. Notably, it saw the largest percentage of de-grossing in two months as well as the largest percentage of net selling on record dating back to 2016.
The firm also said that the move was "driven by long and to a lesser extent short sales."
Intel's sell-off over the last few months may be ending, according to JPMorgan.
The bank upgraded the stock to neutral from underweight, while maintaining its price target of $85. That indicates a 5% loss from Friday's close. Analyst Harlan Sur wrote in a Sunday note that as the stock has approached his price target — as it has declined 36% from its late June peak — the risk/reward profile of the company has improved, though only to become more balanced.
"Since Lip Bu Tan's appointment to CEO, we believe the team's execution and competitiveness in their core client/datacenter compute market has improved, the team's execution on next-gen manufacturing has significantly improved," Sur said in the note. "Despite near-term concerns on AI infrastructure spending sustainability, we believe increasing agentic AI workloads (CPU intensive) and a very tight supply chain for leading edge silicon should drive continued positive EPS revisions in the upcoming earnings season and through CY27."
Shares of Intel were up 4% in premarket trading Monday.
U.S. stocks were on the move Monday morning as investors reacted to fresh earnings, analyst upgrades and corporate developments.
Cleveland-Cliffs surged more than 10% after beating quarterly earnings expectations.
AI-related stocks also attracted attention. Datadog rose 3% after Bernstein upgraded the stock, citing strong AI-driven demand. Amazon climbed more than 1% after Morgan Stanley named it a top pick
Read more on companies making the biggest moves premarket here .
Bank of America Securities issued a double downgrade of Ameriprise Financial to underperform from buy previously, and also slashed his price objective to $445 from $570 that implies the stock should fall another 11% from where it currently is at $500.80.
Analyst Craig Siegenthaler said he expects Ameriprise has started offering bonuses to retain financial advisors, following some large exits, a trend that could start hurting operating margins.
"AMP has seen an acceleration in large team departures to start independent RIAs," Siegenthaler wrote on Monday. "We estimate this has caused AMP to react by offering retention bonuses which could negatively impact operating margins."
"If bond yields are stabilizing, that will help equities, through allowing the cycle to look more sustainable, through reducing pressure on AI funding, as well as on consumer finances, and through reducing the drive for P/E compression," wrote JPMorgan strategist Mislav Matejka. "Indeed, during the most intense phase of yields spiking, forward P/E for AC World fell by 3 points, for SPX by 3 points and for Europe by 2 points. The multiple compression might not need to continue."
Treasury yields pulled back to start the week, while S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures rose following a losing week on Wall Street.
Treasury yields moved lower on Monday as investors continue to weigh the domestic inflation and interest rate backdrop against broader geopolitical developments.
Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — were last seen more than 1 basis point lower to 5.0854%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was also 1 basis point lower at 5.4242%.

articles.title_orig: Tehran seeks to punish Trump in midterms with oil price pain, Iranian officials say
articles.title_zh: Tehran seeks to punish Trump in midterms with oil price pain, Iranian officials say
articles.content_orig:
International Maritime Organization Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez discusses efforts to communicate with Tehran as attacks escalate and commercial shipping faces growing risks.
Thousands of sailors remain stranded near the Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks on commercial ships, the United Nations' top maritime official warned Sunday after Iran accused the U.S. military of using an international emergency radio channel to threaten civilian crews.
The warning also came amid reports that 24 ships had been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, underscoring growing concerns about maritime safety in the region, according to Financial Times .
"The situation continues to be severe and critical when it comes to international shipping," International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital.
"There is a double blockade and too many vessels have been attacked, particularly in recent days.
'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS
Twenty-four ships have been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, according to reports. (Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers have continued to perish in these attacks and around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped since the beginning of the conflict," he warned, adding that his message was not to transit the Strait of Hormuz or put seafarers at risk "until we have guarantees."
Dominguez's warning followed an Oct. 9 letter to the IMO in which Iran alleged that the U.S. military used VHF Channel 16 , an internationally designated maritime distress and safety channel, to intimidate Iranian crews in the Persian Gulf.
"VHF Channel 16 has been repeatedly occupied for prolonged periods by the United States military forces operating in the Persian Gulf," the letter stated.
TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS
Smoke column rises from the tanker El Gaia after an incident in the Strait of Hormuz.
"During such transmissions, Iranian seafarers have been addressed in Persian with threatening, abusive and provocative language and in certain instances urged to abandon their vessels."
In a statement to Fox News Digital, U.S. Central Command defended its enforcement of the naval blockade of Iranian ports .
"The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners," CENTCOM said.
"Vessels that refuse to comply with blockade enforcement receive multiple warnings, with ample opportunity to comply.
"American forces remain highly vigilant, focused and professional while fully enforcing the naval blockade against Iran ."
Iran's complaint was submitted by Seyed Ali Mousavi and its ambassador to the IMO and circulated to member states on Oct. 9, according to a copy reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Tehran also accused American forces of turning the maritime safety channel into an "instrument of military intimidation and psychological pressure against civilian crews."
The letter cited commercial vessels, shipping companies and maritime operators but provided no recordings, transcripts or specific details of the alleged exchanges. Fox News Digital could not independently verify the accusations.
IRAN THREATENS TO HALT RED SEA TRAFFIC IN RESPONSE TO US MILITARY BLOCKADE OF PORTS
Naval units from Iran simulate the rescue of a hijacked vessel during joint drills at the Port of Bandar Abbas in Hormozgan, Iran, on Feb. 19, 2026. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers are not trained for combat, and they are not guilty of any conflicts that are happening around the world," Dominguez said.
"And we have seen this in several parts of the world where Channel 16, that should not be used for this kind of communication, starts receiving messages that may be perceived as actually threatening or that are outside the remit of why it was created."
Iran also asked the IMO to raise its allegations with member states and relevant international organizations, potentially including the International Telecommunication Union.
Dominguez said the IMO could review its regulations and procedures to determine whether stronger safeguards are needed, though he did not announce a formal investigation.
"Our role here at IMO is that when those situations take place, we will then look into any technical measures or any operational aspects that we may need to clarify further within our regulatory framework," he said, stressing that member states have equal rights to raise concerns, regardless of the conflict.
"We have a responsibility, and I have a duty as well, to circulate letters and notes that the countries actually put forward when they're also being affected."
WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS
The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners, CENTCOM said. (U.S. Navy)
"We take all that information, meet at the level of different meetings of the organization and have the discussions," Dominguez added.
"If it's demonstrated that we probably need to improve our rules in order to avoid communications issues, or that we need to enhance the knowledge of how these channels should be used, that is a role for us."
The IMO had recorded 100 confirmed maritime incidents across the region as of Oct. 9, with 24 seafarers killed since the conflict began Feb. 28. Dominguez also warned that fraudulent ship registrations and false flags have become major contributors to the danger.
"What we've also seen right now is an increase in fraudulent registries with false flags that are taking the risk and acting as shuttle tankers in order to bring goods in and out," he said. "That's one of the reasons that we're seeing an escalation.
"And it's the irresponsible shipowners that are taking the risk in order to actually be able to trade and move some of the goods and the cargoes."
WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS
A ship is seen passing through the Strait of Hormuz during a two-week temporary ceasefire between the United States and Iran on April 8, 2026. (Shady Alassar/Anadolu/Getty Images)
"For me, any single case, any vessel that is attacked, any life of a seafarer that is lost, is a critical situation for me, because they are all relevant, they are all important."
Despite the confrontation, Dominguez said diplomatic channels with Iran remain open, though he has no direct contact with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
"I have communications with all the member states of IMO, and that includes the Islamic Republic of Iran," he said.
"Of course, that's through the diplomatic channels. I don't have direct contact with the IRGC .
"I have conversations with them and they respond to my messages. You know, the information flows. What is difficult is to get final decisions because of the conflict that is ongoing."

articles.title_orig: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
articles.title_zh: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the frontlines by drone.
The “historic” mission comes just as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia .
Shared by the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade on Monday, the video shows the soldier strapping himself into a large drone and being flown at what appears to be relatively low altitude over blurred-out territory. The drone carefully lowers him down and the drone operator greets him with “Welcome back to the ground!” The video also showed blurred faces of drone operators who carried out the mission.
The post said the unidentified infantryman was wounded while at his position. “Due to intense enemy drone activity and the presence of landmines, evacuation using conventional unmanned ground vehicles was impossible,” the brigade said.
Injured Ukrainian soldier rescued with a drone
“At that point, the specialists in our unit took it upon themselves to attempt something that had never been done before: evacuating a serviceman using an aerial drone,” it added.
The craft used was a heavy-lift hexacopter, it said, originally designed as a bomber by a Ukrainian manufacturer. It looks about twice the size of the soldier in the video.
The specialists working on the mission had to ensure the drone could carry a human being without flipping over or swaying excessively, according to the unit.
The rescued soldier is currently undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, the brigade added. The squad leader and programmer with the brigade, only identified by his call sign Napalm, called the soldier a “hero” for agreeing to the mission, “having seen and heard the kind of machine that had arrived to get him.”
In a separate statement, Ukraine’s Ground Forces said its drone units are already conducting operations “that were recently considered science fiction.”
The war has increasingly become a technological arms race, with both Ukraine and Russia relying on drones to reduce human casualties.
The conflict has taken a severe toll on both armies, although neither side reports up-to-date numbers of those killed, injured or missing. Ukraine in particular has faced a severe shortage of manpower as it has tried to ramp up recruitment.
Ukraine had a major leap in drone technology this year, allowing it to limit Russian logistics in occupied territories as well as strike deeper inside Russia to target Russian oil refineries , commercial warehouses and data centers .
“This mission proves once again that Ukrainian service members, working in tandem with Ukrainian manufacturers, are setting global trends in the conduct of warfare,” the brigade’s statement added.
Despite hoping that its drone innovation would give it the upper hand at the negotiating table, Kyiv has faced pressure from the U.S. to halt its strikes on Russian oil sites after President Donald Trump signed a diesel deal with the Kremlin earlier this month.
Kyiv has since also reported gaps in intelligence sharing and restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is crucial for its drone missions, battlefield communications and air defense.
The drone evacuation comes just days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the Ukrainian government had approved an “experimental project” to use drones for medical logistics. Koretskyi said flights would require coordination with the military, and drones would be given a special status and would be identifiable in the air.
“During the war, moving medical cargo by road can cost critical time, especially for transplants,” he said. “Drones will be able to carry medicines, medical products, blood samples, and donor organs between hospitals, including from remote areas.”
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Some iPhone Duo orders getting moved up to earlier dates
articles.title_zh: Some iPhone Duo orders getting moved up to earlier dates
articles.content_orig:
iPhone Duo became available for pre-order last Friday, then quickly became backordered into late January 2027. However, a number of users have started reporting that their orders now show earlier delivery dates than originally estimated.
If you ordered an iPhone Duo last week, there’s a chance Apple has just moved up your delivery date—especially, it seems, if you‘re in Japan.
Over the weekend, a variety of iPhone Duo orders in Japan started getting pushed up to earlier dates than Apple originally estimated.
For example, here’s a user whose December date got moved up to October 23.
iPhone Duo、12月着のはずが発売日着に……!? 心とおサイフの準備ができてない！！！ pic.twitter.com/Aw1xepVQLA
Here’s a collection of similar reports found by 9to5Mac’s Dylan McDonald:
Apparently iPhone Duo shipping dates are being bumped up in Japan?? 👀👀 pic.twitter.com/mw8w07tVf8
It is unclear whether this change is going to start rolling out more broadly around the world. Though some orders arriving sooner than expected wouldn’t be surprising .
Apple has yet to comment on the updated shipping dates. It’s possible the improved delivery estimates end up being errors that get reverted, but hopefully that’s not the case.
So far the new dates appear limited to orders directly from Apple. We’ll keep you posted on any new developments to the story.
Has your iPhone Duo delivery date changed at all since ordering? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Uber wins bid to throw out £200m black cab claims
articles.title_zh: Uber wins bid to throw out £200m black cab claims
articles.content_orig:
Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about £340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms.
The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012.
But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true.
Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity.
About 13,000 drivers were seeking nearly £200m in damages, Reuters reported, while a claim on behalf of Kabbie and Iride, two private hire firms that have since closed, sought about £140m.
The lawsuits were filed in 2024, and Uber argued they fell outside the six-year limit for bringing such claims.
In a written ruling, Mr Justice Birt said the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018.
RGL Management, which ran the cases for the claimants, said it was very disappointed and was considering its options with the legal team.
Since gaining its licence, Uber has taken much of the trade once dominated by black cabs.
The company faces a separate case next week, when it challenges HM Revenue and Customs in a tax dispute worth more than £1bn.

articles.title_orig: Priest killed by falling crucifix during live streamed Mass
articles.title_zh: Priest killed by falling crucifix during live streamed Mass
articles.content_orig:
A priest has been killed by a falling crucifix at a church in Ecuador as he performed a mass that was being live streamed online.
Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died on Saturday at the Perpetuo Socorro church in the city of Guayaquil, southern Ecuador, according to a statement from the city’s archdiocese, published on Facebook on Monday.
Video of the incident shows Sánchez leading the mass when a large wooden cross that was standing on the altar behind him falls over and hits him on the head.
Shouting can be heard from the congregation, and several people enter the frame and rush toward the priest.
On Sunday, the church held a eucharist in memory of Sánchez, led by Cardinal Luis Cabrera, archbishop of Guayaquil.
“We are grateful for all of the condolences from around the world, and especially for your prayers for the eternal rest of the soul of Patricio Sánchez,” the statement reads.
According to CNN affiliate Ecuavisa, the priest was preparing to lead a wedding ceremony when the tragedy occurred.
Police have not commented on the incident so far, Ecuavisa reported.
CNN has reached out to the Archdiocese of Guayaquil for comment.

articles.title_orig: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
articles.title_zh: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
articles.content_orig:
Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift . For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced , and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro .
But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.
That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.
I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.
As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)
That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150 . The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines , I thought it sounded kind of fun.
That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.
The best starting place is Relativty VR . This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.
But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD , Project North Star , and the full-body tracking SlimeVR . There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.
A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.
The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders— Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.
Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.
Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.
The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.
Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.
You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.
My total spend for all that came to just under $180.
Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.
I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.
You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.
Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.
Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.
Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.
Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.
As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.
Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.
You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.
That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.
This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in the

articles.title_orig: Saros' Massive Zenith Update Is Available Now on PS5, Free for All Players
articles.title_zh: Saros' Massive Zenith Update Is Available Now on PS5, Free for All Players
articles.content_orig:
Developer Housemarque has just released the Zenith update for Saros , expanding the PS5 shooter with brand new content and features, and it's available now for free.
Weighing in at 3.5 GB, the update brings the game to version 2.0, and it contains various exciting new ways to engage with the roguelite third-person shooter — especially for those that have already completed the campaign.
Overlord Rush is a new boss rush mode. Here, you can take on specific sets of Overlords, or try to tackle all eight of them in a row, and your performance will be measured against other players in online leaderboards.
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
Then there's Eclipse Layers, Saros' version of New Game+ mode. Within the armour matrix you can find new nodes; these unlock the next Eclipse Layer, with each one making the game more intense by introducing new rules.
You'll need to equip Carcosan Modifiers to access Eclipse Layers, and to help with that, 20 new ones have been added — 10 protections and 10 trials — making the selection more varied.
While playing Eclipse Layers, Arjun will don a crown that grows based on how many trial modifiers you have equipped. This crown is also key to finding a new set of collectibles that unlock more lore to enjoy.
New Trophies have been added based on the Zenith update, too.
On top of all that, the update adds more accessibility options to Saros, including the ability to slow the game speed, toggle high contrast visuals, auto-aim, gyro aiming, and more.
There's a bit more detail over on the PS Blog . Will you be jumping back into Saros to explore the Zenith update? Tell us in the comments section below.

articles.title_orig: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down
articles.title_zh: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down
articles.content_orig:
LLMs have led to an explosion of custom firmware and hacks for synths, samplers, and grooveboxes.
If you spend any time on r/synthesizers or watch a lot of synth videos on YouTube, you’ve probably noticed the explosion of custom firmware for hardware synthesizers, samplers, and grooveboxes . What unites almost all of them is that they were made possible by increasingly sophisticated vibe coding tools.
These sorts of custom firmware were exceedingly rare in the pre-LLM days, and required both deep expertise and an incredible investment of time. It could take weeks or months to add a simple feature like velocity sensitivity to a Korg Volca . Now, hobbyist hackers are able to turn Temu synths into full-fledged grooveboxes in a matter of days.
Elektron’s budget-friendly Model:Cycles , Digitone, Octatrack, and Digitakt have all gained new capabilities with Claude’s help. Roland’s SP-404 MKII , Ableton’s Push 3 and Move , Akai’s MPC Live and MPC One, as well as the vintage MPC 2000, Novation’s Circuit, Arturia’s MicroFreak , and even Zoom’s 14-year-old Multistomp pedal line have all seen new custom firmware released in the last month or so.
Leading the charge is a tiny $70 Yamaha DX-7 clone: the M-Vave FM-1 . It was already on its way to being the synth of the summer. The dirt-cheap price and faithful recreation of classic FM tones made it incredibly popular with first-time synth buyers, hobbyists, and synthfluencers alike. Inevitably, someone wondered how far they could push the hardware and, with the help of AI, kickstarted an arms race.
The FM-1 now has dozens of custom firmwares available. Many of the most popular — Felucca , Sloop , and x0x — list Claude as a contributor on their GitHub page or include explicit disclosures about their use of AI. Baudgirl is also suspected to have been created with the assistance of AI, but the developer did not reply to a request for comment.
What started as a surprisingly good, but basic DX-7 clone now supports a variety of synth engines, including virtual analog, sample playback, multi-track sequencing, and a variety of UI designs.
It’s not terribly shocking that someone was willing to risk bricking a $70 Temu synth. Generally, the gear that has benefited from this surge of vibe-coded custom firmware is older or more affordable.
Roman Rusinov, who posts on Reddit as themanro and releases music under Farlow, set his sights on the Zoom MS-70CDR. It’s a budget multi-effects pedal from 2012 that has a reputation for punching above its weight, making it a staple of affordable synth setups. He started by learning about ZDL , a project that reverse-engineered the Multistomp format, allowing for the creation of custom effects. He eventually coaxed the pedal into running NAM A2 Lite captures and custom impulse responses (IRs), turning it into a full-fledged modeler capable of emulating vintage amps.
“I was already using AI for some work stuff and figured this would be a great case to try learning some vibe-coding fundamentals and get a project going,” he told The Verge . “There was a lot of trial and error of finding the limitations of the hardware and software.” He says he’s thrilled to be part of a broader movement. “Somehow it all lined up with all these other projects pushing the boundaries of older hardware and breathing new life into it. I love that,” he said. “If you own the hardware, you should be able to do whatever you want with it.”
18nelli, the developer behind Modded Cycles , was similarly motivated by a desire to revitalize some forgotten gear. “I had an Elektron Model:Cycles that left me feeling frustrated,” he told The Verge . He said that it felt designed “just to push us to buy their more expensive gear.” But recent AI advances made him believe he could add features to the groovebox, which hasn’t had an official update since May 2021.
So he opened up his Cycles, documented all the parts, and started working with Claude Code to implement his first hack — six-track audio over USB. That has since exploded into a community project with multiple mods contributed by others, several standalone custom firmwares , and even the ability to turn your Model:Cycles into a Model:Samples. “I think not using LLMs would have been counterproductive,” he said. “I probably would have spent a massive amount of time and energy on just a single feature, whereas my real goal is to actually create and make music with amazing mods.”
Modded Cycles has certainly been one of the more frantic projects out there. I recently watched as five firmware updates hit the announcements channel on its Discord in one day. 18nelli has since said he plans to pause adding new features and slow development to polish the existing code and stomp out some bugs.
New mods and firmwares hit the web almost every day now. If there’s a favorite piece of gear in your arsenal that you wish had one killer feature, there’s a chance it might end up on a GitHub page sooner than later. Heck, if you just wish your pocket synth could play NES ROMs , that’s also a distinct possibility.
Of course, there is some risk here. These firmwares are often less thoroughly tested than the manufacturer’s official one. The response to the modding scene has varied from company to company, with many choosing to remain silent. Elektron banned links to custom firmware from their forums. In a statement posted on its official forums, the company said, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them … Something that looks like a simple change in isolation can lead to major problems elsewhere, particularly when a later official OS arrives, and can confuse users about which features are officially available on our machines.”
Others, like M-Vave, seem to be embracing the movement. It recently announced FM1 Open , an open-source firmware with additional features, plus a development kit and a firmware-flashing tool for the community.
The response to music gear that uses AI and vibe coding has been mixed. Devices like the Polyend Endless have sparked some ire . And music-making subreddits are awash in people complaining about vibe-coded plugin slop . But so far the community has been less hostile to vibe-coded firmware. Maybe, in part, because breathing new life into old instruments helps keep their Gear Acquisition Syndrome (GAS) in check.

articles.title_orig: Musk pledges 1 SpaceX share for every child in America
articles.title_zh: Musk pledges 1 SpaceX share for every child in America
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk has said he will give every child in America a stake in SpaceX, his $2 trillion aerospace and artificial intelligence company, as tech firms face intensifying scrutiny over their impact on society.
“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” he wrote on X on Monday. “This will be the first of many.”
SpaceX only began trading publicly in June (and had the biggest initial public offering in history ). The company’s shares were trading for about $146 when the market closed on Friday.
Musk’s proposal was thin on detail. It is not clear how those shares would be distributed to the tens of millions of American children or whether all of them would even be eligible.
According to the United States Census Bureau, there are roughly 73 million people under the age of 18, making Musk’s potential giveaway worth about $10.7 billion at SpaceX’s current share price.
Offering young people a stake in the US stock market isn’t a new idea. This month, the Treasury Department automatically signed up millions of under-18s to Trump Accounts, a new federal savings and investment vehicle, with children born between the start of 2025 and the end of 2028 eligible for a one-off $1,000 government contribution.
Musk’s offer came in response to Anthropic’s announcement on Sunday that it will commit at least 5% of its shares — worth $48 billion at the private company’s latest valuation — to a “Public Benefit Fund” that will donate money to social causes.
The fund could make “large donations” to non-profit organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations,” the company wrote on its website, adding that the money could help mitigate the impact of artificial intelligence on people’s jobs.
Musk retorted on X : “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public…  This is what I will be doing.”
Both offers come as AI companies face intense backlash over the safety of their products (Anthropic itself recently warned of the “existential risk to humanity” posed by the technology), the potential for AI to push humans out of their jobs en masse, as well as the social and environmental impact of the industry’s gargantuan data center build-out.
Tech titans more broadly are catching heat.
New movies like “The Social Reckoning” — about a Facebook employee blowing the whistle on unsafe company practices — and documentary “You Can See Everything” — following blood testing start-up founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes — are helping to remind audiences of the long-running recklessness of some in Big Tech.
Musk himself is the subject of the new documentary “Musk,” charting his life and career. It is unsparing in its criticism of some of his business practices and controversial foray into politics.

articles.title_zh: Nobody should buy the $299 Apple TV 4K, but it could have been worse
articles.content_orig:
My colleague Zac Hall described HomeView as one of the best ways to spend $299 on an Apple device and the Apple TV 4K as the worst . Almost nobody thinks anyone should buy the latter at that price, but things could have been even worse …
1st gen 4k doesn't support the latest OS so those users (ME) get to buy the new device and after 9 years of use, I feel like I've gotten my money out of it and don't mind spending the $ for the next years of use.  :)
The 4th-gen Apple TV 4K has been launched at an eye-opening price of $299 (and only a little less on Amazon). You do get some new features for your money, including built-in microphones, an upgraded remote, and support for surround sound with the HomePod mini 2. But the tech world consensus appears to be that almost nobody should buy this model, especially given you’ll get Siri AI support with a 2nd- or 3rd-gen box. You can buy entire large-screen TVs for less.
Tech journalist Glenn Fleishman put together a chart showing that the price increase is well above inflation when upgrading from almost any of the previous models. That’s true from the 2nd-gen Apple TV, which went on sale at $99, through to the 3rd-gen Apple TV 4K at a launch price of $129.
But the same comprehensive chart also shows that things could have been very much worse. The very first Apple TV box went on sale at $299 way back in 2007. Adjusted for inflation, that’s the equivalent of $491 today …

articles.title_orig: Toulouse to Ho Chi Minh City: Five fast-rising cities that should be on travellers' radars right now
articles.title_zh: Toulouse to Ho Chi Minh City: Five fast-rising cities that should be on travellers' radars right now
articles.content_orig:
A new global report spotlights the world's emerging urban hotspots. From thriving cultural scenes to changing neighbourhoods, locals reveal what makes them worth exploring now.
New York, London and Paris have once again topped Oxford Economics' annual ranking of the world's leading cities . But beyond these familiar names, its 2026 Global Cities Index has identified 28 " cities to watch " – places whose rapid growth and rising fortunes could see them become increasingly influential in the years ahead.
These cities aren't just growing economically. New neighbourhoods, thriving cultural scenes and improved transport links are already reshaping the visitor experience and making them increasingly interesting places to visit.
We selected five from the list and spoke to people who know them well to find out what's changing – and why they're worth exploring now.
With its population forecast to grow by 57,000 over the next four years – more than anywhere else in France – Toulouse is one of Europe's fastest-growing cities and is attracting younger, skilled newcomers with its mild climate, relatively affordable cost of living and high quality of life.
"Here, you don't have to choose between slow life and fast life," said Elodie Paramelle, who recently returned to Toulouse after 10 years in London. "You get the energy of a big city, with an incredible food scene, independent cafes, cocktail bars and a growing cultural offering, alongside a much slower pace of life."
Toulouse has changed significantly in recent years, according to Mélodie Tyler, who moved back here after seven years in Paris. She says the city is much more walkable and bike-friendly, while its food and wine scene has expanded dramatically. And she notes that the buzz is spreading beyond the historic centre. "Ponts-Jumeaux where I live hosts a bunch of festivals, guinguettes [open-air bars] and skateboarding competitions," she said. "The Toulousains love to party and be outside as much as possible!"
Beyond its thriving neighbourhoods, Toulouse is also major aerospace hub, home to hundreds of companies, including Airbus's global headquarters. Visitors can explore that heritage at the Cité de l'Espace space-themed discovery centre or Aeroscopia aviation museum beside the Airbus runways. For something more unusual, La Halle de La Machine brings art and engineering together through giant mechanical creatures created by a local street theatre company.
Vietnam's largest city is on a remarkable trajectory. Oxford Economics predicts Ho Chi Minh City will be among the world's 50 fastest-growing cities over the next five years, with an economy that could rival Berlin's by 2050. Tourism is booming too, with more than eight million international visitors last year, exceeding projections.
"The first metro line only opened at the end of 2024, and it's one of the most tangible symbols of how quickly the city is changing," said Meaghan Yash, a travel specialist at tour operator Timbuktu Travel who frequently designs trips here. The 20km (12.5 mile) line runs from Ben Thanh Market in the city centre to the Suoi Tien theme park, with single fares costing less than £1 ($1.33).
Yet, Ho Chi Minh's appeal lies in how it balances change with continuity. Chris Buchart, commercial director at Vietnamese hotel company Fusion Group, suggests travellers visit the French-colonial Central Post Office and Opera House , and then the War Remnants Museum for context on the country's history, before turning to one of the city's greatest strengths: its food.
Buchart recommends trying bánh mì (Vietnamese baguette sandwich) , cơm tấm (broken rice) and bánh xèo (crispy pancakes), while Yash suggests venturing beyond the usual tourist circuit in central District 1 to quieter, more residential neighbourhoods where leafy streets are ideal for wandering and cafe-hopping. He also suggests Chợ Lớn, the city's historic Chinatown, for its markets, temples and medicine shops, while across the river in Thảo Điền, independent boutiques, galleries and home-grown Vietnamese brands make for excellent shopping.
The Polish capital has made one of the fastest jumps in the Global Cities index, climbing more than 100 places to 61st. Its quality-of-life score now surpasses London, New York and Tokyo, while its economy is projected to expand by around 3% annually – nearly twice the European city average.
For Konrad Warzecha, a Polish-Australian whose family home is in Warsaw's Wola district, the transformation has been remarkable. "From our balcony you can see the skyline, and watching the roads, highways and towers go up over 20 years has made the city almost unrecognisable," said Warzecha, who blogs at House Sitters Guide .
The biggest changes, he says, are on the streets. "As a kid I rode the trams and did not feel safe, and I saw many robberies happen," he said. "Now I have never felt safer. People walk around at night, the streets are clean and trouble gets dealt with quickly."
For first-time visitors, Warzecha recommends a walk that takes in both the old and new city. He starts at the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science and follows Nowy Świat boulevard into the Old Town , painstakingly rebuilt after World War Two.
Along the way, he stops for pączki (Polish doughnuts) and a meal at a bar mleczny, one of the city's traditional, no-frills milk bars. "It tastes like home cooking," he said. "A three-course meal with drinks comes to around £13 ($17).
Warzecha once wanted to leave Poland and move back to Australia, but today his feelings have changed. "These days Warsaw is one of the places I recommend most, and not because I am from there. I am proud to have a Polish background."
Medellín's remarkable transformation is reflected in its economic fortunes. Employment in business and financial services has more than doubled over the past 20 years, and Oxford Economics predicts that the Colombian city's average income will overtake Buenos Aires and São Paulo by the 2040s.
"In the 10 years I've lived here, Medellín has gone from a curiosity for only the most daring to a hub for travel," said Patrick Quinn, who runs the Colombia Writers Retreat in nearby El Peñol. "Once blighted or overlooked places like Comuna 13, Perpetuo Socorro and Ciudad del Río have become cultural and economic centres."
The city's Metrocable , the first urban cable car system designed for mass public transport, carries commuters and visitors up the surrounding hillsides, while emerging creative districts are giving travellers new reasons to explore. "There is enough happening in its food, art and design scenes to warrant several days in its own right," said Joanna Rigby Jones, a travel specialist at Timbuktu Travel who has planned trips here for years. She recommends the creative district, Perpetuo Socorro , for design shops, galleries and speciality coffee.

Comuna 13 , once one of the city's most dangerous districts, now draws some of Medellín's biggest crowds. "Go with a local guide who can provide the context behind the murals, escalators and music rather than treating the neighbourhood simply as an Instagram backdrop," said Rigby Jones.
Quinn also recommends exploring the Poblado and Laureles neighbourhoods, seeking out local creators and curators. "That way, you can go home and tell stories that will dismantle outdated misconceptions about this place," he said.
Once heavily dependent on oil, Abu Dhabi has transformed its economy through investment in technology, renewable energy, property and finance. The UAE capital now ranks sixth in the Global Cities index for the skills and education of its workforce, ahead of Paris and Boston, while its non-oil economy and job market are projected to surpass neighbouring Dubai.

articles.title_orig: Nintendo "Underestimated" Zelda Switch 2 Console Sales, But Promises Restocks Are On The Way
articles.title_zh: Nintendo "Underestimated" Zelda Switch 2 Console Sales, But Promises Restocks Are On The Way
articles.content_orig:
If you are anything like us, the reveal of the special edition Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2 console last month was quickly followed by the dreaded realisation of "oh no, I need this". Alas, for many, this need has not been fulfilled, with supply shortages making those all-important pre-orders far rarer than we'd like them to be.
In a recent interview with YouTube channel Coelho no Japão , Nintendo's Latin America Vice President and General Manager Bill van Zyll admitted that the company had "underestimated" the demand for the console, and reaffirmed that further restocks are on the way (thanks for the heads up, GamesRadar+ ).
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 853k
"It's a global phenomenon; we have this issue everywhere," van Zyll told the YouTube channel, "we apologise for that. That certainly wasn't the intent".
"We underestimated how well it would be received," van Zyll continued, "and there are certainly some markets that stand out" — he explicitly mentioned North America as one such market.
However, it's not all doom and gloom. Nintendo has made it clear in the weeks since pre-orders went live that more products will be made available down the line, and van Zyll banged the same drum in this interview. "We are working on replenishments of the special hardware and software, but it'll take a little bit of time," he confirmed, before dealing out the old Nintendo chestnut: "Please be patient".
Here in Europe, we have seen the system come in and out of stock at various retailers in recent weeks, and we're sure it's a trend that'll continue on the run-up to launch. Considering how popular just about every SE Switch 1 console was in the past, we're a little surprised that Nintendo wouldn't expect the same from * checks notes * a gold, Zelda-themed Switch 2 , but hey, here we are.

articles.title_orig: US issues rare Middle East red alert warning to its citizens in the region
articles.title_zh: US issues rare Middle East red alert warning to its citizens in the region
articles.content_orig:
US embassies across the entire Middle East issued identical security alerts on Monday, warning their citizens in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Yemen and Iran to exercise heightened vigilance.
The alerts warn all US citizens of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions due to the risk of military escalation linked to Yemen’s Houthis and Iran.
The warning covering 12 countries states that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area” and to “develop contingency plans in advance.”
“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions,” the alert said.
In Saudi Arabia, the embassy warned of a “complex security environment,” as “Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions.”
The alert also states that “Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions.”
In Qatar, the US embassy urged its citizens on Sunday to monitor official alerts and local media, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, and follow instructions from local authorities.⁠
Qatar Airways announced on Monday that it will suspend its Saudi-bound flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until 24 October and reduce flights to Jeddah from seven to four per day.

articles.title_orig: Credit stress is threatening to unwind the AI bull. All eyes are on Oracle to hold the line
articles.title_zh: Credit stress is threatening to unwind the AI bull. All eyes are on Oracle to hold the line
articles.content_orig:
Oracle bonds are sitting dangerously close to junk territory as markets cool on artificial intelligence. Much of the AI trade fizzled last week, led by CoreWeave — the neocloud company whose equity and debt has been tanking .
Oracle now faces risk of credit rating downgrades that could tip its debt into junk territory — with potentially cascading effects across the AI financing ecosystem.
"There seems to be a sentiment shift, which almost speaks to 2026 in general, where we're so bullish about everything and then we're so bearish about everything," said Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners. "It just shows you how quickly this market moves."
But there are key differences between CoreWeave and Oracle — the latter is investment grade while Coreweave is already in junk territory. Some analysts and fixed income investors tell CNBC they aren't concerned yet about Oracle and the other hyperscalers.
Still, the shift in sentiment can be seen in the spread of Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The range is more in line with BB and B credit, which is high yield, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
The spread on Oracle's five-year CDS is currently 295 basis points, after briefly hitting 300 bps on Thursday, up 287% in one year.
"Oracle CDS is supported by high liquidity. Nonetheless, its spreads whipsawed over the last few days, no doubt a reflection of the fragile sentiment in AI-related names, notably those in HY [high yield] and at the weaker end of the IG [investment-grade] spectrum, such as Oracle," he said in an email to CNBC.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
Oracle's rating is S&P Credit Ratings is BBB-, the lowest level in the investment-grade spectrum. The agency downgraded Oracle in July, noting that the company's rapidly expanding infrastructure business is increasing its overall credit risk. S&P also said it expects weaker operating cash flow in 2027.
Oracle is primarily an enterprise software company but it's barreling into data centers and cloud services, including a massive $300 billion deal with OpenAI. To fund the buildout, Oracle has issued $118 billion in long-term debt and has another $39 billion in capital and lease obligations, according to FactSet data.
The spending and debt obligations are taking a toll on Oracle's finances while the company waits for a gusher of AI revenue. Analysts estimate free cash flow of -$23.7 billion this year and -$36 billion in 2027, according to consensus forecasts.
That would be bad enough for investors, but Oracle is more than just a debt-laden data center play. It's become an AI "bellwether," notes Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank. A downgrade of its credit into junk territory "would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," he said in a report.
S&P said in its July downgrade that another downgrade could be triggered by: an expectation that Oracle will sustain leverage exceeding 4x; or belief that the software company isn't on a path to generate positive free operating cash flow by fiscal 2029; or a negative view on Oracle's AI strategy or that of the overall AI industry.
As an investment-grade company, Oracle can borrow cheaply and with duration, but that would change with a junk rating, said Jamie Meyers, a senior securities analyst at Laffer Tengler, which owns Oracle stock.
"Nobody in high yield is going to buy a 30 year debt," he said. "Getting downgraded to junk would mean that they'd have to push everything short. Obviously, their borrowing rate would be higher, more than likely."
That said, Meyers is not concerned about Oracle's debt levels. In a meeting between Oracle and Laffer Tengler last year, Oracle stressed it will defend its investment-grade rating, Meyers said.
"We do believe the revenue is going to start ramping and the earnings are going to start ramping," he said. "What Oracle really needs is … time. They need to get these things built."
Brad Collins, a fixed income portfolio manager at Vanguard, also expressed confidence in Oracle and the other hyperscalers.
"Oracle is most under the microscope, but as a result, has been more diligent in their issuance" so far this year, he said. "Balance sheets are in a healthy starting spot, and [I] would not extrapolate what we are seeing in HY to IG."
The company's current troubles could be looked at as a "financing test," said Dynasty Financial Partners' Nerney. They'll either pass or fail, which could mean an additional downgrade, he said.
"The real question now is, with the move in rates, how much is that going to cost?" he said. "If rates continue to move higher, just the opportunity cost of investors to hold Oracle paper relative to other things in the market, you're going to see the market demand more."
Oracle responded to a request for comment by saying, "We have been very clear that maintaining an investment grade rating is our first priority as a company."
"The AI infrastructure business has strong economic returns and we expect it will produce strong free cash flows once projects are ramped," it added.
