articles.title_orig: Roche returns to China’s Hansoh for $15B biobucks ADC pact
articles.title_zh: Roche returns to China’s Hansoh for $15B biobucks ADC pact
articles.content_orig:
A year after their first antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) team-up, Roche has returned to Hansoh Pharmaceutical for a mammoth $15 billion biobucks pact.
The latest agreement spans a “broad portfolio of ADC programs,” Hansoh explained in an Oct. 19 release. They include two ADCs already in preclinical development at the Chinese biopharma, along with multiple programs focused on targets suggested by Roche but powered by Hansoh’s ADC tech.
The plan is for Jiangsu-based Hansoh to take these programs through phase 1 trials, before passing over responsibility to Roche to develop the ADCs worldwide—excluding Greater China.
In return, Hansoh will receive $400 million in upfront cash, followed by $110 million on the first anniversary of the deal. Further down the line, the biopharma is in line for potentially up to $15 billion in development, regulatory and commercialization milestones, as well as tiered royalties on sales if any ADCs make it to market.
The deal also has a clause where Hansoh could opt to contribute toward the global development of two programs from the collaboration. If it picks this route, Hansoh would become eligible to receive “incremental upside from the commercialization of these two programs,” according to the release.
This morning’s deal comes a year after Roche handed $80 million to Hansoh and pledged $1.45 billion in biobucks for the ex-China license to a CDH17-targeted ADC, dubbed HS-20110. At the time, HS-20110 was already in phase 1 testing in China and the U.S. as a potential treatment for colorectal cancer and other solid tumors.
“Building on the ADC partnership we announced last year, we are delighted to further strengthen our collaboration with Roche,” Eliza Sun, Executive Director of Hansoh’s board, said in this morning’s release.
“This new agreement reflects our shared commitment to advancing ADC innovation and underscores our strategy of leveraging our deep expertise to accelerate the development of transformative therapies for cancer patients globally,” Sun added.
Boris Zaïtra, head of corporate business development at Roche, said in this morning’s release that“expanding our strategic collaboration with Hansoh marks an important step in advancing our ADC vision.”
“Exploring next-generation ADCs is one of the most compelling frontiers in oncology today, offering the opportunity to address critical unmet needs and accelerate potential therapies for patients worldwide,” Zaïtra added.
Roche isn’t the only Big Pharma that’s turned to Hansoh to help power its ADC ambitions. GSK has already tasted clinical success with a pair of ADCs aimed at B7-H3 and B7-H4, respectively.
The B7-H3-directed ADC, dubbed ris-rez, recently achieved a median overall survival of 18.5 months in a phase 3 trial, lining up the therapy as a potential threat to Amgen and Merck & Co. in the lung cancer field. Last night, GSK unveiled the first global data for ris-rez, which demonstrated a 61% overall response rate in a phase 1b trial.
Jefferies analysts said that the readout helped move ris-rez from a therapy defined by its “impressive China phase 3” data to “a much more globally validated asset story.” Ris-rez is “starting to look like the B7-H3 ADC to beat in relapsed SCLC,” the analysts concluded.
Hong Kong-listed Hansoh has been one of the leading lights in China’s emergence as a biopharma innovation engine, notching collaborations with the likes of Merck & Co. and Regeneron . In August, Hansoh offered a bullish assessment of China’s innovative biopharma sector, arguing (PDF) that the industry is “fully transitioning from the ‘follower’ phase to the ‘frontrunner’ phase.”
This year, Hansoh stepped up spending to support its pipeline of more than 40 innovative medicine candidates that it is assessing in more than 70 clinical trials. R&D spending at the company jumped 20.7% to 1.7 billion Chinese yuan ($253 million) over the first half of the year.

articles.title_zh: I ate 12 burritos in SF, LA and SD. There's one I still think about.
articles.content_orig:
Christopher is a freelance writer who has been writing about technology for almost two decades. Previously editor-in-chief of technology website Pocket-lint.com, Chris is an expert in TVs, smartphones and all forms of connected tech.
The products or services listed have been independently tested by our journalists. We earn a commission from the affiliate links in this article. Read more >
Any tablet users who try to use their device in bright light will be familiar with the dreaded glare; where streaming and reading anything on screen becomes a strain (on both the eyes and one’s patience). The premium model in Amazon’s new range aims to solve the issue, for far less than Apple’s machine with an equivalent screen.
The tech giant is updating and replacing its keenly priced Fire tablets – at the budget end of the market, features wise – and replacing them with Amazon Alexa Tablets, designed to compete with the iPad. There are eight and 11-inch models, but it’s the 12-inch Alexa Pro that has caught my eye. While Amazon is pushing the AI capabilities (of which more later), it’s the matte screen that allows reading the likes of e-books, emails – or dare we say it, The Telegraph digital edition – in bright light much easier (and in a bigger format, which is preferable to squinting at a smartphone).
Priced at £499.99, it’s more expensive than any of Amazon’s previous tablets, but it’s £250 cheaper than the iPad Air, which doesn’t benefit from a matte screen. It’s also £600 cheaper than the iPad Pro, the only model in Apple’s line-up that has a comparable screen.
Amazon calls it a ‘Nanomatte display’ and it’s similar to the ‘Nano-texture’ display on the much more expensive iPad Pro . The aim is to reduce reflections for better visibility across the display. I found it really effective at stopping reflections from windows and indoor lights. Being next to a train window in sunlight would make it easier to catch up with Bake Off glare-free, for example. It also retains visibility in direct light outdoors, though there will always be an element of glare on any device in the brightest light. In those conditions, I’d advise seeking some cover where you can. I found it works very well under an umbrella in the garden (as it would on a shaded sun-lounger). It delivers a better reading or working experience than all but the most expensive iPad.
This device feels frictionless, so when swiping your fingers across the display, they glide perfectly smoothly. It’s a subtle difference to a glossy screen, but it feels a lot more premium. At the same time the colours remain bright and vibrant, with plenty of detail in images and text, while graphics and animations look nice and fluid too.
I should say that a matte display on a tablet is rare. It’s available on the iPad Pro, but Apple only offers this on the 1TB storage model and charges an additional £100. That means the cheapest iPad you can get with a similar display is £1899. With that device, you are paying for a powerful machine that can handle the likes of video editing and 3-D modelling, which will certainly be overkill if you just want your tablet to handle entertainment and lighter work tasks.
TCL has more comparable tablets with its “Nxtpaper” display, available for around £220 . However, those lack the power and features of the more expensive rivals.
For dedicated Kindle users, the difference will be welcome. When using the app there are several different display modes, automatically changing the screen to look more like paper, while also turning on the blue light filter and silencing notifications. It’s designed to strip away distractions so you can focus on the book you’re reading – and it looks great.
That said, at 555g, the Alexa Tablet Pro is a lot heavier than standard Kindles , which are around the 200g-mark and light to hold with one hand. Personally, I wouldn’t replace my Kindle Paperwhite, but it’s a good back-up option.
For anyone who uses their tablet for email and web-browsing, there are a range of accessories. There is the Pro Keyboard (£129.99) and a Pro Pen (£79.99). I tried the keyboard and found the trackpad to be responsive and the keys to support a nice typing action.
Amazon says that this tablet has three times the computing power and nine times the graphics power of any previous Amazon tablet, so this is a significant boost in performance to previous models.
That will make light tasks, such as crunching through emails, browser-based activity like online shopping and document work. With a keyboard factored in, it could work as a laptop alternative for some. The same could be said of the iPad Air, although with recent price increases from Apple and the matte screen, for my money, this is a better proposition.
The premium makeover that comes with the Alexa Tablet Pro includes a slim aluminium design, with flattened edges, so it looks like an iPad or Samsung tablet, only 6.5mm thick. The Pro version only comes in the Graphite colour seen here. All models in the new line-up feel more grown-up and less like kid’s tablets than the Fire range. Plus the switch to proper Android over Fire OS is welcome and will result in better app compatibility (although I noticed that these tablets were running Android 16, which is now an old version).
It has a battery that’s good for 16 hours of video playback and supports 27W charging. There are cameras front and rear although like any tablet, these won’t be as good as your phone, while there’s support for Dolby Atmos from the speakers, so your movies will sound decent.
As the name suggests, Amazon is keen to promote the AI element here. It has customised the interface slightly with access to Alexa+ meaning you can utilise Amazon’s AI at any time to ask about what’s on the screen, to control smart home devices or search for content. If you are a keen Alexa user, then that will be a plus, but for me it’s not the headline news.
With the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro , Amazon has an Android tablet that’s a lot more competitive against devices from Apple, Samsung and Lenovo that dominate sales.
I think it will particularly appeal to users who turn to a tablet for both entertainment and work or admin tasks and are sick of screen-based travails. For die-hard Apple fans who want things synchronised across their phone, tablet and laptop, it may be a harder sell.
The Alexa Tablet Pro with Nanomatte display costs from £499.99 and it’s available to pre-order now, with shipping from 19 October.

Senior Business Strategy Manager at Microsoft (Xbox), Brandon Stirrup, has recently taken to social media to address the elephant in the room: AI . Having spent his weekend creating what he calls his “ little bad game ” with no prior experience in game development, Stirrup has made a bold acknowledgment that Western fans likely won’t be happy to hear.
Look if I’m fired tomorrow it will be because I told you the truth that nobody wants you to know. You can make a game with a simple prompt and yes you can make custom, tailored games. Everything you want in a game is right there for the taking, for better or worse.
It is true, mind you, that you can prompt a game into existence. The quality of those games will always be up for debate, but it’s no secret that the barriers to entry for game development are shrinking, whether for better or worse, as Stirrup says, with an apparent sense of unease.
Stirrup argues that the gaming industry is uniquely resistant to this shift. “ Gaming is the only industry slow-walking the transition because users have negative sentiment. Everyone else accepts reality ,” he claimed.
He also added , “ Gaming is the only industry where leaders are afraid to talk about ai. Users want the truth. We’re using AI. ”
It’s quite the admission, but it doesn’t come as a surprise, at least to me. While Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has been rather hesitant to fully embrace AI, we did just recently get Xbox Labs , an initiative to explore AI-driven game development and modding.
For what it’s worth, I hope Stirrup doesn’t get fired over these comments . As weird and scary as AI can be, I imagine many developers are using it, even ones you might not expect, like Capcom , which has admitted to its use .
The issue comes down to how AI is being used. As good a tool as it is, developers still need to understand what is being created by AI; otherwise, you end up with a hotbed of spaghetti code, which just leads to more issues down the line.
Do let me know how you feel about Stirrup’s comments. Do you agree, disagree, or land somewhere in the middle? And don’t forget to take part in our poll!

articles.title_orig: ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’: What does the French student protest slogan mean?
articles.title_zh: ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’: What does the French student protest slogan mean?
articles.content_orig:
It has been scrawled on cardboard placards outside blockaded schools, shared in parody videos tens of thousands of times and repeated by Greta Thunberg. In the space of a few weeks, "Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres" has become the unofficial slogan of France’s high school protests.
Taken literally, the phrase means very little, and that is the point.
"Bismillah" is Arabic for "in the name of God". Muslims traditionally say it before beginning a task, and in everyday French slang it can mean something closer to "let’s go".
"C’est les ténèbres" translates as "it’s the darkness". Among young people it is slang for a situation that is catastrophic or grim.
Put together, the phrase is nonsensical - "In the name of God, it’s the darkness". Students say that is exactly why it caught on. They are mocking someone trying, and failing, to sound like them.
The phrase comes from a screenshot of a Snapchat conversation that began circulating in early October, while students were using the app to organise school blockades.
In the message, a user named "Mamadou" asks to join a group: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?"
The message was accompanied by Algerian flag emojis.
Other screenshots showed similar accounts asking students where blockades would take place and who was selling fireworks and smoke grenades.
To many students, the clumsy mix of Arabic, street slang and national flags gave the game away. They concluded that the messages were written by police officers posing as teenagers to infiltrate private protest groups.
This has not been proven. Neither the police nor the interior ministry in France has commented on the screenshots, and nobody has independently verified who was behind the accounts.
Some internet users claimed to have traced the accounts to locations near police stations, but those claims have not been verified. Some of the circulating screenshots may themselves be hoaxes or parodies.
The movement began in Créteil, south-east of Paris, on 18 September and quickly spread nationwide. A range of student grievances lie at the heart of the movement , including long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down schools and teacher absences.
Many argue that these problems hit working-class suburbs and minority communities hardest. Around 400 schools were closed by blockades on 2 October alone.
The student protests fed into the nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living on Saturday 17 October, which ended in some of the worst rioting and looting France has seen in years.
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg used it during a visit to striking students in Seine-Saint-Denis, north of Paris, on 13 October, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
On 9 October, it appeared on placards at a union-led demonstration in Brussels against the Belgian government’s budget cuts. There, it was used as a gesture of solidarity with French students rather than a reference to the infiltration claims.
In Italy, ANSA reported that the phrase appeared at student demonstrations in Bologna on 15 October. It was heard again in Milan over the weekend of 17 and 18 October, when protests in Piazza del Duomo also turned to looting and students from a french school in Berlin were photographed holding a banner of the slogan.

articles.title_orig: US and China compete for influence in Central Asia
articles.title_zh: US and China compete for influence in Central Asia
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in Uzbekistan promoting trade and ties with Central Asia
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in Uzbekistan on Monday to promote trade and ties with Central Asia, during a trip that came amid rumblings that America’s top diplomat is ignoring pressing matters in favor of politically safer visits and meetings.
The trip, which involves a stop in India later this week, seeks to promote U.S. economic and security ties with Central and South Asia . But it has only tangential links to the Trump administration’s current main foreign policy dilemmas in the Middle East and with the Russia-Ukraine war .
Rubio has brushed aside suggestions he is eschewing the most difficult issues in favor of taking on lower-hanging diplomatic fruit with less risk of failure and political damage, and the State Department pushed back on the criticism of his schedule.
In Samarkand, Rubio was meeting with his counterparts from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan under the C5+1 diplomatic forum, which brings together the five Central Asian countries and the United States to discuss security, trade and other shared concerns.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the meeting, Rubio said “the United States wants to be a strong partner in Central Asia.”
“Central Asia has just not gotten the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now,” he said.
Despite repeated assurances from multiple administrations that the U.S. would become more actively involved in Central Asia, the region has often languished as a foreign policy priority in Washington.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the newly independent Central Asian nations saw a brief surge in U.S. interest, but that waned until after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States, which turned America’s attention once again toward Afghanistan and its neighbors.
The U.S. established a military presence in several countries mainly as transit points for equipment, materiel and provisions needed by U.S. and allied forces fighting the Taliban and al-Qaida in Afghanistan.
As the U.S. wound down its 20-year operation in Afghanistan, the Trump administration, in both its first and second terms, has sought to elevate its ties with Central Asia due to its location between Russia and China, but also as an underdeveloped area ripe for U.S. business opportunities.
Rubio’s trip, which has been heavily promoted by the U.S. ambassador to India and special presidential envoy for Central Asia, Sergio Gor, is perhaps the most ambitious U.S. attempt in decades to boost economic and commercial ties with the region. Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Rubio described “an incredible delegation” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining.
“Historically, Central Asia has been the crossroads for trade between the West and the East. And today, as part of a broader renaissance and global engagement, it stands once again to play that vital role in transnational commerce," he told officials at the meeting.
The region is "a new location for investment, and it serves as a new location for export, a central terminal out of which materials that are vital for the future of all nations are being delivered,” he added.
President Donald Trump hosted their leaders at a White House summit last November, and announced more than $130 billion in commercial deals, including agreements for regional airlines to purchase Boeing aircraft.
The administration has also been keen to get the Muslim majority countries to join the Abraham Accords, which expanded the number of Arab states with diplomatic ties with Israel. Kazakhstan, which had already recognized Israel, is the only one of the five to sign the accords .
Associated Press writer Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.title_zh: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.content_orig:
A California woman who prosecutors allege was spying on a son of Taiwan’s president was indicted this month on charges of conspiracy and being an unregistered foreign agent for China.
The indictment was filed Oct. 9 in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the allegations it lays out mirror an earlier criminal complaint against the woman, Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine.
Prosecutors say Zhang, who also goes by Heather, spied on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his home in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. The spying is alleged to have taken place between roughly June and September 2025, prosecutors claim.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that is the source of 90% of the world’s “leading-edge chip manufacturing,” according to the U.S. International Trade Administration . China claims Taiwan, which the U.S. has no official relationship with , though it is required by law to ensure Taiwan can defend itself.
Prosecutors allege Zhang was under the direction of an unnamed Chinese government official and former classmate at her alma mater, China’s University of International Relations, which is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus,” an FBI investigator said in earlier court documents.
An example of the alleged activity was a request by the former classmate to send him pictures “of the house” where the son lives, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors alleged that Zhang flew from California to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area to conduct surveillance of the unidentified son and his home from outside.
The indictment alleges she captured photos, video and license plate information and sent them to the person alleged to be her Chinese handler. An unidentified person, who had fled to China in September, was with her, prosecutors said.
Zhang also traveled to China in August 2025 to meet with a Chinese government official, returned days later and told the official she would most likely be going to where the victim was the following week, according to the indictment.
Her lawyer, Craig Harbaugh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
Previously, Harbaugh, a veteran criminal defense attorney, described Zhang as an upstanding resident of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of Los Angeles, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said in court Oct. 7.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Sunday.
Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry, said this month after Zhang was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport that he was “not familiar” with the situation and that Beijing “opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative.”
U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim ordered Zhang held in pretrial detention after prosecutors argued she poses a flight risk. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons website shows that she remains in custody.
Zhang is scheduled to appear in federal district court Friday for a post-indictment arraignment. She could face up to 15 years in prison.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Australian MP Helen Haines critically injured in ‘deliberate’ car ramming
articles.title_zh: Australian MP Helen Haines critically injured in ‘deliberate’ car ramming
articles.content_orig:
An Australian lawmaker is in a critical condition after being hit by a car outside her electorate office in what the Prime Minister says was a “deliberate act,” though police are yet to identify a motive.
Helen Haines, 65, who represents the federal seat of Indi, was struck by a Toyota Landcruiser in Wangaratta, a rural city in northeast Victoria, about 3:30 p.m. local time on Monday, according to Victoria Police and her family, who identified her in a statement.
Witnesses rushed to her aid and detained the vehicle’s 43-year-old driver until police arrived, according to Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason. A knife was found during a search of the car, Mason added.
Political violence is rare in Australia, but reports of harassing and threatening behavior against politicians had risen in the past year, according to Australian Federal Police (AFP) statistics cited by the government.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told state broadcaster the ABC late Monday it appeared to be a “deliberate act,” and while he wasn’t aware of any individual threats against Haines, he said the “temperature” of political discourse had “increased in recent times” and urged it to be turned down.
“There’s no place for political violence in a democracy,” he added.
A multi-tiered investigation is underway involving the AFP, Victoria Police, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) and the Joint Counter-Terrorism Team to examine the motive behind the attack.
Haines was elected to federal parliament in 2019 as an independent candidate who fought for better healthcare services in rural areas. She stood for integrity in politics, and called for gambling reform, better mental treatment and an end an to the war in Gaza.
Before entering politics, she worked as a midwife, establishing one of the country’s longest running rural midwifery services, according to her website.
“Helen Haines is incredibly hardworking,” Albanese said at a press conference on Monday. “She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity, and respected right across the Parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her.”
As he spoke, police officers were at the scene of the incident, working within a cordoned area near Haines’ electorate office on the main road in Wangaratta, a rural city home to around 30,000 people.
Police haven’t named the suspect but say he was from Tarrawingee, a rural town about 12 kilometers (seven miles) east of Wangaratta. It’s not clear if he was known to Haines, police said.
Politicians from all sides of politics expressed their shock into the evening on Monday. Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor said it was a “shocking day for the nation.”
“Australians will be angry and appalled by the attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta,” he posted to X. ” Our nation cannot become a place where violent attacks are normalised.”
Pauline Hanson, leader of the right wing One Nation party that’s risen in popularity in recent months, also said there was no place for violence against any elected representative.
“Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety,” she said on X.

articles.title_orig: Israeli police arrest 10 over settler attacks on journalist and diplomats in West Bank
articles.title_zh: Israeli police arrest 10 over settler attacks on journalist and diplomats in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Israeli police arrested 10 people Monday as part of an investigation into violence that included the beating of Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine while she was reporting in the occupied West Bank.
The arrests follow an attack that left Levine, a longtime photojournalist, with serious injuries and prompted calls from the Washington Post and U.S. officials for accountability. Police did not identify the suspects or say which, if any, were directly involved in Levine's assault, according to the Washington Post .
Levine was attacked Friday while covering a Palestinian olive harvest near the West Bank village of Abu Falah. Witnesses said masked Israeli settlers knocked her to the ground, repeatedly kicked her and beat her with sticks despite her wearing protective gear clearly identifying her as press.
She suffered broken ribs and vertebrae and underwent surgery on a badly injured finger. Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray condemned the assault and called for a thorough investigation.
Levine has spent decades covering conflicts across the Middle East and elsewhere, including the wars in Iraq, Afghanistan and Ukraine.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called the attack a "despicable act of terror" and said those responsible "should spend YRS in prison." He said the U.S. had called for a full investigation, arrests and prosecution.
Monday's arrests were part of a wider investigation into violence over the weekend that also included an attack on European diplomats near the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh. Israeli police said the operation involved the military, Border Police and Shin Bet.
The suspects were taken in for questioning. Police have not announced charges or publicly detailed what role each suspect is believed to have played in the attacks.
The arrests come three days after Levine's beating drew attention to the risks facing journalists covering unrest in the West Bank and renewed calls for Israeli authorities to identify and prosecute those responsible.

articles.title_orig: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.title_zh: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
French officials are exploring introducing curfews as the country reels from its worst rioting in years after protests over education and the cost of living spiraled into a wave of deadly, country-wide violence that has sparked a blame game at home and threatens to spill over into its European neighbors.
Over the weekend, police fired tear gas into crowds and fought running battles with black-clad, hooded rioters who set fires and broke into shops and government buildings, with images showing historic buildings ablaze.
The mood in the country remained tense on Monday, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asking some cities to impose “partial curfews” to protect people, property and businesses. In Marseille, officials banned all gatherings and demonstrations from midday until 8 p.m. local time in anticipation of any more flare-ups, while protestors blocked access to the Louvre Museum in Paris, forcing it to close.
Those measures were introduced after more than 2,000 people were arrested this past weekend, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands. As France begins to count the cost, accusations are mounting that the government failed to adequately anticipate the scale of the crisis, with an election to succeed French President Emmanuel Macron just six months away.
The vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, authorities and political leaders stress – but the level of fighting and destruction , the worst seen in years, has shaken the nation and prompted forceful condemnations from leaders and the public alike.
“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said on Sunday evening. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”
He also promised to hold meetings this week to discuss “concrete proposals” and to listen to protesters’ demands. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to stem the protests in France – as well as similar demonstrations against costs of living now spreading in other countries nearby.
It started in September with a strike by students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs, who demanded more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.
Students around the country, long frustrated with an understaffed and overcrowded education system, launched protests that at times turned violent. A heavy-handed police response fueled public anger and pushed hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets, especially after videos of a police officer using a banned headlock on a girl.
Within a few weeks, the protests swelled to become a broader movement beyond students, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.
“This can’t go on,” said 57-year-old Maria Pallas, a member of a major French trade union, speaking to CNN at Saturday’s protest in Paris. “There’s the cost of living. There’s unemployment. There’s a bunch of things. A young person will go looking for work, we’ll promise him a lot, and he’ll end up with nothing.”
Over half a million people demonstrated across France on Saturday. For the most part, things were peaceful; far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the crowd in Paris as “moving calmly.”
But in several locations the protests spilled into violence, especially as night fell. In Paris, groups of masked young people looted shops and started fires; in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office; in the central city of Limoges, the spire of a 143-year-old town hall collapsed in flames, reviving painful memories for some of the Notre Dame Cathedral fire. Hundreds of businesses were vandalized across the Île-de-France region, which includes Paris, a local business representative told BFMTV.
The protests subsided somewhat on Sunday, with small pockets flaring, and police firing tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, one of the largest public squares in Paris.
By the end of the weekend, Paris looked like a “war zone,” one visitor to the city told Reuters. Residents across the capital were stunned, with some condemning the looters and rioters, and others placing blame with authorities who failed to address the crisis earlier.
“It’s heartbreaking, heartbreaking seeing our city like this,” said 59-year-old Marseille resident Farida, who did not give a last name, according to Reuters. “If every protest ends with all the shop windows smashed and stores trashed, this simply cannot go on — it cannot go on.”
One Paris resident, 56-year-old Paola Formenti, voiced support for the protesters’ “legitimate” anger, even as she condemned the violence.
In his Sunday address, Macron acknowledged protesters’ grievances and said he would take “a number of international initiatives” to tackle fuel prices and ensure a stable supply from Gulf nations. He did not make any concrete assurances or give further specifics.
Even interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted authorities had failed to anticipate the scale of the riots and offered his resignation, though Macron refused to accept it.
The protests and fallout could shape France’s upcoming election next spring. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed this weekend that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Mélenchon, has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.
Protesters have taken to the streets elsewhere in Europe this weekend, too.
In Belgium, students demonstrated against the state of their education system. In Lisbon, Portugal, tens of thousands of people marched on Saturday to protest rising costs of living and the country’s housing crisis.
In Italy, Milan also saw two consecutive nights of unrest this weekend. Protesters threw stones and looted supermarkets, while police responded with tear gas, and water cannons, and arrested 32 people.
Meanwhile in Albania, students have been taking to the streets for months, protesting perceived government corruption. Demonstrations in the capital Tirana turned violent this weekend, with one person photographed throwing a Molotov cocktail at riot police.
Authorities in many of these countries have condemned the violence and called for calm. The protests have caught the attention of the White House, with Vice President JD Vance posting a video of the burning Limoges town hall on X and blaming the unrest on failed immigration policy.
US President Donald Trump also mentioned the protests during a rally in Georgia this weekend, joking: “Let’s go to France and join the revolution and spend our $5,000 there,” referring to the dividend promised if the Republicans win the midterm elections.
CNN’s Joseph Ataman, Niamh Kennedy, Lisa Courbebaisse, Lucie Lepellec, Catherine Nicholls, Sana Noor Haq, James Legge, Sharon Braithwaite, and Melissa Bell contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China Lectures Israel on the West Bank: What About Tibet?
articles.title_zh: China Lectures Israel on the West Bank: What About Tibet?
articles.content_orig:
Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in Israel
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left the Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.
Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, was set upon last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupied West Bank towns.
The photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground,” Levine said. “Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me.” She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
Huckabee, a rightwing ally of President Donald Trump with a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine. In a post on X on Saturday, he noted that she was a US citizen who had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”
Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu , has been ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.
In an interview with the Associated Press on Sunday, Levine said she had been “shocked and insulted” to hear that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as “alleged”, adding that the prime minister “had all the evidence on the table”.
But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, and in a letter signed by several of the country’s top former security and intelligence officials, in which they all expressed shame over the attack.
Levine blamed “Jewish terrorists” for Thursday’s attack and added: “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today.”
The photojournalist also said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries. “I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this,” she said. “They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
The attack on the Palestinian farmers and Levine was followed on Saturday by another outbreak of settler violence directed against European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of the French city of Cambrai, who were visiting the occupied West Bank .
Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground. A masked militant shouted “Vive la France!” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Baudoux told Agence France-Presse after he was attacked. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening. For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.”
Violence is surging ahead of bitterly fought elections to be held on 27 October, with Palestinians’ annual olive harvest being repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement rightwing base.
France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has called on Israel to “urgently halt criminal violence” and to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux. The EU has condemned the attack and urged “full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists”.
The European Commission executive vice-president, Teresa Ribera, went further, posting an interview with Levine in hospital and adding the caption: “They want no witnesses.”
Israel’s foreign ministry has condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
On Monday, Israeli ⁠police said they have ⁠arrested ⁠eight ​suspects as part of an investigation ⁠into violent incidents in the West ⁠Bank over the weekend. The police did not identify the suspects.
Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, called Levine in hospital on Saturday, saying the attack was “outrageous and shocking” and was weighing on his conscience.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the elections, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, criticised the prime minister over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses”. He described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in a post on his Truth Social network on Sunday, hailing him as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He added: “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
The Washington Post has reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation into the attack on Levine, even though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.
Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says about 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Computational analysis ‘solves’ what Mario 64’s infamous plaque says, and it’s not ‘L is Real 2401’
articles.title_zh: Computational analysis ‘solves’ what Mario 64’s infamous plaque says, and it’s not ‘L is Real 2401’
articles.content_orig:
A Super Mario 64 fan has performed an open-source computational analysis in an attempt to finally solve the game’s infamous ‘L is Real 2401’ mystery.
For around 30 years, players have tried to figure out what the plaque on the fountain in Peach’s Castle says in the 1996 Nintendo 64 launch game.
An early theory was that the plaque reads, ‘L is Real 2401’, a potential hint that Luigi might be playable in the game and that 2401 might be a clue on how to unlock him.
In 1996, IGN.com offered $100 to anyone who could figure out how to unlock Luigi, while in its April 1998 issue, Nintendo Power magazine mentioned the ‘L is Real 2401’ theory in an April Fool’s Day feature.
Modern re-releases of the game featuring sharper visuals haven’t made the answer any clearer, since the original plaque text was only written on a small 32×32 pixel tile.
Now programmer Mochi64 has performed a complex analysis on the plaque in an attempt to finally decode what it says, and made their results open-source for others to check.
According to Mochi64, because the two lines of text are 3-5 pixels tall, they’re too small to read, so any attempt to upscale the image is pointless because it’s just guesswork.
Instead, their process used millions of calculations to figure out what combination of words, font, and resizing technique that would have been performed by an artist in the mid-90s would have resulted in pixels closest to those in the plaque.
Using this process, Mochi64 believes the message actually reads ‘Eternal Star’ on the top line, and ‘We Hope So’ on the bottom line, because this provided the closest possible match after millions of comparisons.
Mochi64 applied a scoring system to their tool, which grades each word and phrase on how close a match it is to the original texture. After trying more than 1.2 million words, the above received the lowest (and therefore best) mismatch score of 1,129. By comparison, ‘L is Real 2401’ had a mismatch score of 2,031 on the first line alone.
Mochi64 has also posted a ‘plaque challenge’, where people can use the same open-source code to test another phrase and see if they can get an even lower score, but after their fairly exhaustive process they’re sure this is the definitive answer. As for what it actually means, Nintendo seems unlikely to ever confirm.
Luigi was originally intended as a second playable character in Super Mario 64, according to a 1996 interview with director Shigeru Miyamoto , which is what sparked fascination with the game’s blurry sign.
Speaking via an official strategy guide, Miyamoto described “a room made of simple Lego-like blocks” in which “Mario and Luigi could run around in there, climb slopes, jump around, etc”. This seems to match YouTube footage from a 1995 expo appearing to show the two characters together.
According to Miyamoto, Luigi stayed in Super Mario 64 until the final year of development, after which they removed him due to memory issues.
“We were going to include him in a Mario Bros. style minigame, but because most users probably only have that one controller when they first buy their N64, for that reason (and others) we decided not to,” Miyamoto said at the time.
We finally have a glimpse of what the early multiplayer mode for Super Mario 64 looked like! This is also the first time we have seen Luigi's SM64 model outside of the Nintendo Leaks! Take a look! pic.twitter.com/Ev3R7NDBtp
“I think it would have been great if we’d been able to make it two-player, with Mario and Luigi. But if we had done it wrong, it would have turned into a fighting game or something (laughs), so we’re leaving that challenge for next time.”
In a 2009 Iwata Asks interview , Miyamoto commented again on the canned Mario 64 multiplayer mode, saying: “The screen was split and they went into the castle separately. When they meet in the corridor, I was incredibly happy! (laughs) Then there was also the mode where the camera is fixed and we see Mario running away, steadily getting smaller and smaller.”
If authentic, the Space World 1995 footage is the first documented time Luigi has been seen in the classic N64 game, outside of a high-profile 2020 leak of classic Nintendo game files , which included a model for the character.

articles.title_orig: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
articles.title_zh: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
articles.content_orig:
From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout — millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life.
“I ended up in a situation where I had absolutely no money. Well, I had the money, but it was inaccessible,” said Irina, a blogger from St. Petersburg, who had not been able to access her money for four days when she spoke with NBC News last week.
Irina, who like several other interviewees did not want her last name shared while speaking with a foreign news organization on a sensitive matter, said her rent was due the day the first outages happened, when she hoped “that it would be fixed in a few hours.” Days later, she still had no access to money to pay for utilities or even food for her small child.
The strikes that took place over several days earlier this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers as Ukraine seeks to bring the war home for Russians .
The disruption hit a myriad of services provided by Yandex, a tech giant akin to Google whose services are deeply integrated into daily life in Russia, and whose digital infrastructure is relied on by other third-party platforms.
Many people took to social media to complain about not being able to order a taxi or food delivery. Others reported not being able to access their files on the company’s storage service, while some even struggled to get into their homes after their digital keys went offline.
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.
Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.
Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that the company is working to restore service.
“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”
Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between the southern city of Krasnodar and Moscow, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.
“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has two million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before,” she added.
Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages, and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.
She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them, this came from the outside.”
Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, a 30-year-old barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after being unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.
She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay, but said the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.
Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they couldn’t see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He was originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.
Another driver, Valery from Krasnodar, had only been on the job for a few months, having previously worked at a packing center for Wildberries, Russia’s retail giant, whose warehouse was attacked by Ukrainian drones in July.
When the Yandex outages started, he said the taxi app would show error messages or even send several cars for the same customer.
While that has been largely resolved, Valery said the biggest issue for him was that he couldn’t withdraw the money that he had already earned with Yandex. “If I can’t access my pay in another week or two, I will start looking for another job,” Valery, 24, said.
In addition to Yandex, the data centers of Russia’s biggest bank Sberbank and tech giant VK have also been targeted in recent days.
That chaos is no accident, analysts say. “Ukraine’s campaign from the start has had as one of its objectives bringing home to ordinary Russians the fact that they are at war, and this involves consequences,” Keir Giles, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told NBC News.
The aim, Giles said, is for everyday Russians to conclude that their lives are being disrupted because of their leaders’ actions in waging war.
Yandex may also be a target because of its role in shaping what Russians see online, said Robert Tollast, a drone expert and researcher at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
Data centers also have growing military value, Tollast added, as both sides use battlefield data to improve operations and commanders’ situational awareness, potentially with AI-assisted planning.
Asked about the outages and whether the government was looking into financially assisting those affected, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was premature to talk about government support because Yandex is “facing difficulties,” but is “strong and powerful.” Meanwhile, Russian authorities were looking at protecting data centers after the “unprecedented attack,” said Minister of Digital Development Maksut Shadayev.
On Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin held a meeting on enhancing the level of digital security in Russia, but Peskov said it was not linked to the attacks on data centers.
Russia has increasingly ramped up its own attacks on Ukrainian data centers, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet.” Ukraine was reciprocating those strikes by hitting Yandex, he said in a speech last week, adding without providing evidence that “it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms” because there were fewer Russian bots around. NBC News could not verify if Yandex services going down had that effect.
While both sides have hit data centers, Russia’s were an easier target, said Mykhailo Samus, a Ukrainian military analyst and director of the New Geopolitics Research Network.
While Ukraine’s data centers are widely dispersed, many of Russia’s are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, he said, meaning a strike on a single site can disrupt services spanning transport, internet access and payments.
“Very easy and very important,” he said.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Meet the researchers leaving the US because of Trump's funding cuts and politicization of science
articles.title_zh: Meet the researchers leaving the US because of Trump's funding cuts and politicization of science
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Halley Froehlich never expected to leave the United States, where her family lineage stretches back to the 1700s, to pursue her scientific career.
Yet, faced with stalled federal grants and growing uncertainty over the country's research environment, she packed her life into boxes and relocated to Finland alongside her husband and daughter. She now studies how climate change affects edible fish, shellfish, and seaweed at the University of Helsinki .
Her departure reflects a wider trend. When the Trump administration began reshaping the American scientific sector last year by altering the federal grant distribution process and seeking greater political influence over funded projects, foreign academic institutions recognized an opportunity.
Many introduced dedicated schemes designed to entice U.S.-based scholars by offering stable financial support and academic freedom.
A growing number of academics have accepted these international offers. Though comprehensive nationwide data remains difficult to aggregate, university officials, researchers, and professional associations describe the ongoing shift as clear, unprecedented, and concerning.
"You can almost talk to any vice president for research at a university and they will tell you of one or two top faculty that they’ve lost," said Tobin Smith, senior vice president of government relations and public policy for the Association of American Universities.
White House spokesperson Liz Huston said Trump is "ending waste" and is "committed to keeping America the world leader in scientific innovation, and that means funding real science."
Despite those assurances, an April report from the Business for Federal Research Funding Coalition revealed that more than half of U.S. states have lost scientists to recruitment programs in other countries.
Survey data from last March indicated that early-career biomedical scientists were about 20 percentage points less likely to say they wanted to stay in the U.S. "now" than they did six months earlier.
Furthermore, figures from the American Institute of Physics show that physics Ph.D. graduates in 2025 departed the U.S. at the highest rate observed in 30 years.
Institutions in nations such as Canada , France , Belgium , and Finland are publicly advertising their success in drawing scholars from U.S. organizations. For a country that far and away leads the world in Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, and chemistry, researchers view this as a disturbing and surprising development.
"It used to be the shining city on the hill where we all want to go," said Christine Stawitz, now at the University of Birmingham in England . "That reputational loss, I think, is hard to quantify, but also really damaging."
Stawitz stepped down from her job at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration last year to become a research software engineer in the United Kingdom .
She noted that NOAA no longer aligned with her values, particularly after receiving directives to strip websites of references to climate change and diversity, equity and inclusion topics.
She added that the state of American science has become a recurring topic of conversation at international gatherings. " People talk about the U.S. at conferences in the U.K. now like, I don't know what's going on there. It's not good," she said.
For Froehlich, the choice to relocate developed over time. Already concerned by issues surrounding school safety and gun violence in the U.S., she watched as the national research landscape was overturned.
At the University of California, Santa Barbara, grant postponements and cancellations left colleagues struggling and student researchers in tears. Doubts regarding future federal backing for her climate-focused research mounted.
"The cumulative effect of those things ultimately ended up making us really serious about, I don’t think here is our home anymore," said Froehlich.
She ultimately accepted an offer through an initiative by the Research Council of Finland, securing five years of guaranteed funding totaling about $3 million. She moved into a flat by the Baltic Sea in Helsinki and is taking university-sponsored Finnish lessons.
Foreign researchers who were drawn to the U.S. for its reputation as a global leader in science are also seeking different places to do their work.
Married biologists James Letts, who is Canadian, and Maria Maldonado, who is Argentinian, left their academic positions at the University of California, Davis to join Australia 's Monash University. Both earned their doctoral degrees in New York and spent over a decade doing science in the U.S.
Grant-related uncertainty—including laying off a staff scientist while waiting for stalled funding—motivated them to make the move.
"All I want to do is do great science and make discoveries, but I want my work to mean something as well. And the opportunity to do that seemed very difficult in the U.S.," Letts said.
Immigrants have historically won 40 percent of the U.S. science Nobel Prizes. However, Omar Yaghi, a 2025 Nobel Prize winner for chemistry, departed his position at the University of California, Berkeley this year to direct an artificial intelligence lab at China’s Tsinghua University.
The U.S. remains a science powerhouse, full of institutions with robust research communities and well-resourced facilities that attract foreign talent.
Even if every European country threw open its doors, there still would not be enough capacity to accommodate every American scientist. Many researchers are choosing to stay, searching for new sources of funding or pivoting to industry positions.
Nevertheless, concerns persist regarding the ongoing erosion of reputation and talent. The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to $174 billion in federal grants since the president's second term began, according to tracking data compiled by the States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness.
Additionally, a proposed rule from the Office of Management and Budget could accord political appointees more control over which future projects are funded, though a resolution approved by Congress has delayed a final decision on the rule until December.
Scientists who have moved away and those remaining in the U.S. are worried about what lies ahead. They warn that the next generation of scientists may face fewer graduate programs, diminished funding, and reduced mentorship—effects that could take a decade or longer for the U.S. scientific enterprise to fully feel.
Major research institutions accepted 15% fewer applicants for fall 2026 doctoral programs compared to last year, according to admissions data collected by the Association of American Universities. One of the impacted students was a mentee of Smith's.
"What is one of my pieces of advice to that young man? Next year, look in Canada," he said.

articles.content_orig:
How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Switch 2 revised model retains old LCD panel, teardown confirms no Sharp upgrade
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Switch 2 revised model retains old LCD panel, teardown confirms no Sharp upgrade
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo has introduced a new version of the Nintendo Switch 2 in Europe, bringing a hardware change that could make the handheld console easier to maintain over time.
The updated model features a user-replaceable battery, allowing owners to swap out the battery themselves instead of relying entirely on professional repair services.
The change addresses a common concern with portable gaming devices: battery capacity gradually declines with repeated charging and years of use. However, a teardown comparing the original Nintendo Switch 2 with the new European model suggests that the update focuses primarily on repairability rather than gaming performance.
Although the revised console features changes to its internal components, it reportedly retains the same NVIDIA processor and 12GB of RAM.
For current owners, that means there may be little reason to upgrade, while first-time buyers could benefit from the easier battery replacement.
The most significant feature of the updated Nintendo Switch 2 model is its replaceable battery, according to Digital Trends .
Unlike handheld consoles that require extensive disassembly or specialized repair work when their batteries deteriorate, the new version is designed to make battery replacement more accessible to users.
Rechargeable batteries naturally lose capacity over time. As a result, an older handheld console may provide shorter gaming sessions even when its other components continue working properly.
A replaceable battery could help extend the useful life of the Switch 2 by allowing owners to replace a worn battery rather than replace the entire console. It may also make long-term maintenance more practical for players who use their devices frequently.
However, the available teardown information does not establish the exact replacement procedure, battery pricing, or whether Nintendo will sell replacement batteries directly to consumers in every market.
Read more: Deadlock Violet Brings Terrain Control and Second Economy to City Never Sleeps
A teardown shared on X by user modyfikatorcasper compared the original Switch 2, identified as BEE-CPU-01, with the newer OSM-CPU-01 model.
The examination revealed several internal differences, including a redesigned motherboard, a different cooling fan, and a replaceable battery.
Despite these changes, the two consoles reportedly use the same NVIDIA chip and contain 12GB of RAM. The newer version sources its memory from a different supplier, but the teardown did not indicate an increase in memory capacity.
These findings suggest that Nintendo has revised the console's internal design without substantially changing its core hardware specifications.
The updated motherboard and other components may show efforts to simplify manufacturing or make repairs easier, although the exact reasons for each redesign have not been confirmed.
Based on the reported teardown, the new Nintendo Switch 2 hardware revision does not offer an obvious performance improvement over the original model.
Both versions reportedly retain the same processor and RAM capacity. The examination also found no clear evidence of improved graphics capabilities or a more powerful cooling system.
Consequently, players should not expect the newer console to deliver higher frame rates, sharper graphics, or significantly faster loading times simply because of the revised internal components.
The different fan and motherboard do not automatically indicate better cooling or processing performance. Additional testing would be necessary to establish whether the revised hardware changes temperatures, noise levels, power consumption, or sustained performance during demanding games.
The practical difference is therefore expected to be easier battery maintenance rather than a better gaming experience.
There have also been reports suggesting that the updated Nintendo Switch 2 could feature a display manufactured by Sharp.
However, the unit examined by modyfikatorcasper reportedly retained the original display panel. The teardown therefore did not confirm that Nintendo had switched display suppliers across the updated model.
Further examinations of additional units would be needed to determine whether different display panels appear in other versions.
For buyers, this distinction matters because a change in display supplier does not necessarily mean a visible improvement in brightness, color reproduction, resolution, or power efficiency. Those characteristics would require separate testing.
The new model also appears to weigh slightly more than the original Nintendo Switch 2.
According to the reported measurements, the original console weighs approximately 400 grams without controllers and around 534 grams with the Joy-Con 2 controllers attached.
The revised model weighs approximately 410 grams without controllers. With the Joy-Con 2 attached, it is reportedly around 12 grams heavier than the original.
The difference is relatively small, although players who frequently carry their consoles or play in handheld mode may notice it when comparing both versions directly.
The available information does not establish precisely which redesigned components account for the additional weight.
For people who already own the original Nintendo Switch 2, the updated model offers limited reasons to replace a functioning console.
The reported hardware specifications remain largely unchanged, and there is no confirmed improvement in graphics or overall gaming performance. Unless easier battery replacement is particularly important to an owner, the benefits may not justify purchasing another console.
The situation is different for first-time buyers. A user-replaceable battery could make the updated model a more practical long-term purchase, particularly for players who intend to keep their handheld console for many years.
However, availability, local pricing, warranty conditions, and the actual battery replacement process should be considered before making a purchase decision.
The updated European model reportedly features a replaceable battery, a redesigned motherboard, a different fan, and a different memory supplier. It retains the same NVIDIA chip and 12GB of RAM.
The new model is designed around a user-replaceable battery. However, the exact replacement procedure and availability of official replacement batteries may vary, so buyers should consult Nintendo's regional guidance.
There is no confirmed evidence from the reported teardown that the revised model offers improved graphics or higher gaming performance.

Most existing owners have little reason to upgrade if their current console works well. The main advantage is easier battery replacement rather than a confirmed performance improvement.

articles.title_orig: US threatens Europe with ‘devastating’ retaliation if EU restricts SpaceX’s access to European market
articles.title_zh: US threatens Europe with ‘devastating’ retaliation if EU restricts SpaceX’s access to European market
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder told the Financial Times that European companies would face “devastating” retaliation from Washington if Brussels moves forward with plans to restrict American competitors’ access to parts of the European market.
The dispute centers on a European Commission proposal to reserve part of the radio spectrum that lets smartphones connect directly to satellites for European companies, a move that would restrict spectrum access for Chinese and American companies, including SpaceX.
Asked whether European companies should fear retaliation, Puzder said they “should be wary that it could happen and it would be very devastating for those companies,” given the size of the American market.
Puzder said that if the goal “is to make United States less competitive, I think that that’s not a legitimate goal of this kind of legislation.” “You don’t make European companies more competitive by making US companies less competitive,” he added.
SpaceX has sharply criticized the European Commission’s proposal, warning that the move risks degrading communications quality in Ukraine, where Starlink plays a critical role.
On October 14, Ukrainian military officials reported restrictions affecting the operation of Starlink satellite communication terminals, or more precisely, their military version, Starshield. The restrictions emerged amid growing tension between Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump, who, however, claims he did not order the terminals’ operation restricted. The Telegraph’s sources said that SpaceX head Elon Musk proposed restricting Starlink’s operation in Ukraine to Trump, and the U.S. president agreed.

articles.title_orig: Rubio Confirms Talks Are Underway About Possible U.S.-China-Russia Summit On Ukraine War
articles.title_zh: Rubio Confirms Talks Are Underway About Possible U.S.-China-Russia Summit On Ukraine War
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. Such a summit may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to the report.
The call also produced a deal for Moscow to sell diesel on the global market.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said early Monday that "there's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear," he said in comments reported by Reuters.
"The president is open to anything that he can do to help bring a war to an end, if it's possible, and we'll continue to look for opportunities to do that," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.
It comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer. Over the past week, a series of moves by the Trump administration has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. It caused alarm among European allies and prompted criticism from fellow Republicans.
Over the weekend, Trump defended his decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as well as an executive order on Oct. 18 to waive new Russia sanctions from a bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Trump and Zelenskyy have traded criticism over how to end the war in Ukraine, with Trump accusing the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace , while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia risks prolonging the conflict. In a post on X, Zelenskyy said that ″the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me."
The tensions come as Russia launched another wave of overnight attacks on Ukraine, firing 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones across the country, according to Zelenskyy.
In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy said the strikes damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities, leaving at least 550,000 households without power. He also said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its partners about the missile attacks. Casualties were reported, while a medical clinic, school, metro station and residential buildings were also damaged.
The latest move comes after Trump told Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that it was driving up diesel prices.
A so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Oct. 11 saw Moscow continuing strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure. Ukraine had then paused strikes for three days, but resumed attacks again last Thursday.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote on Sunday.
On Sunday, he also told Bloomberg that "steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate."
"I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."
Over the weekend, both Kyiv and Moscow traded strikes, with Ukraine launching a strike of over 1,000 drones into Russia, setting fires at an oil export terminal and refinery in the city of St Petersburg, while Moscow pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Last week, Kyiv also accused Washington of ordering restrictions on its Starshield networks, the military grade version of SpaceX's Starlink which it uses to control military forces and defend against Russian strikes.
Trump denied on Friday that the White House had ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government."
The restrictions meant that platforms that traveled above 160 kilometers an hour (100 miles an hour), such as interceptor drones, had lost connectivity.
Ukrainian media reported Zelenskyy as saying that the restrictions were a "planned operation," as Ukraine had sent cars with Starlink to EU countries to test Starlink's connectivity, and discovered that there were no such restrictions in those countries.
Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.
The Telegraph reported on Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: French Government-Bond Yields Rise on Protests, Budget Concerns; Treasury Yields Fall
articles.title_zh: French Government-Bond Yields Rise on Protests, Budget Concerns; Treasury Yields Fall
articles.content_orig:
France's parliament begins debate on the 2027 budget Tuesday as high deficits, rising debt and student protests sharpen the political cost of fiscal consolidation.
The euro zone's second-biggest economy is barreling toward a debt crisis, and risks dragging the continent down with it, unless it sustainably brings down its national deficit, according to many market watchers.
Even as thousands take to the streets to protest years of underfunding in public services, particularly education, France has run one of Europe's highest deficit-to-GDP ratios for nearly a decade under President Emmanuel Macron.
Government spending remains well above its peers in the politically sensitive realm of social protections, particularly pensions and healthcare, while tepid economic growth has failed to compensate.
With presidential elections looming next year and parliamentarians proving reluctant to compromise, France's economic and political uncertainty is weighing on the euro .
French government borrowing costs have soared to their highest level in nearly a quarter of a century as jittery bond markets have responded to the country's failure to impose fiscal consolidation.
The widening gap in French bond yields over their German equivalents has raised questions over whether the European Central Bank would have to take the expensive and politically controversial step of intervening to stabilize the market. While this could halt a panic that fragments the currency union, the legacy of the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which hammered countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy — means it would require drastic action from France.
"The ECB will not step in just to 'bail out' France. If there was a European crisis they will intervene in some form but they will not save a country that cannot save itself," Antonio Fatas, professor of Economics at INSEAD Business School, said by email.
